title: Basic Sentence Structure
description: Learn how English sentences are built: Subject + Verb + Object.

lessons.heading: The Foundation of Every Sentence
lessons.text: Every complete English sentence needs a subject (who or what) and a verb (the action). Many sentences also have an object (what receives the action).
examples: I eat rice.
She reads books.
They play football.

lessons.heading: Subject
lessons.text: The subject is the person or thing doing the action. It usually comes first in a sentence.
examples: I run.
The dog barks.
My mother cooks.

lessons.heading: Verb
lessons.text: The verb is the action word. It tells what the subject does.
examples: I eat.
She sleeps.
They study.

lessons.heading: Object
lessons.text: The object receives the action. Not all sentences need an object.
examples: I eat rice. (rice = object)
She reads a book. (a book = object)
He drives a car.

exercises.hint: action of putting words on paper

title: Tenses (12 Tenses)
description: Master all 12 English tenses — present, past, future, and their continuous, perfect, and perfect continuous forms.

lessons.heading: Overview: The 12 Tenses
lessons.text: English has 3 time frames (present, past, future) × 4 aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) = 12 tenses. Each tense changes the verb form to show WHEN and HOW an action happens.
examples: I write. (present simple)
I am writing. (present continuous)
I have written. (present perfect)
I have been writing. (present perfect continuous)

lessons.heading: Present Simple
lessons.text: Use for habits, routines, general truths, and permanent situations. Form: subject + base verb (+s for he/she/it).
examples: I wake up at 7 AM every day.
She works in a hospital.
The sun rises in the east.
They play tennis on Sundays.

lessons.heading: Present Continuous
lessons.text: Use for actions happening right now, or temporary situations around now. Form: subject + am/is/are + verb-ing.
examples: I am reading a book right now.
She is studying for her exam.
They are playing football.
We are staying at a hotel this week.

lessons.heading: Present Perfect
lessons.text: Use for past actions with a result now, life experiences, and actions that started in the past and continue. Form: subject + have/has + past participle.
examples: I have lost my keys. (result now)
She has visited Paris three times.
They have lived here for five years.
Have you ever eaten sushi?

lessons.heading: Present Perfect Continuous
lessons.text: Use to emphasise the duration of an action that started in the past and is still happening. Form: subject + have/has + been + verb-ing.
examples: I have been studying for three hours.
She has been reading that book for a week.
It has been raining all day.
They have been waiting since 2 PM.

lessons.heading: Past Simple
lessons.text: Use for completed actions at a specific time in the past. Form: subject + verb-ed (regular) or irregular past form.
examples: I visited Paris last year.
She watched a movie yesterday.
They went to the beach.
He ate lunch at noon.

lessons.heading: Past Continuous
lessons.text: Use for actions in progress at a specific past time, or interrupted actions. Form: subject + was/were + verb-ing.
examples: I was watching TV at 8 PM last night.
She was reading when I called.
They were playing football when it started raining.
The sun was shining and birds were singing.

lessons.heading: Past Perfect
lessons.text: Use to show that one past action happened before another past action. Form: subject + had + past participle.
examples: I had already eaten when she arrived.
She had finished her work before the meeting started.
They had never seen snow until they visited Canada.
The movie had already started when we got there.

lessons.heading: Past Perfect Continuous
lessons.text: Use to emphasise the duration of an action that continued up to another point in the past. Form: subject + had + been + verb-ing.
examples: I had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.
She was tired because she had been working all day.
They had been driving for five hours when they stopped.
It had been raining all night.

lessons.heading: Future Simple (Will & Going To)
lessons.text: Use 'will' for spontaneous decisions, predictions, and promises. Use 'going to' for plans and evidence. Form: subject + will + base verb / subject + am/is/are + going to + verb.
examples: I'll help you with that.
It will rain tomorrow.
I am going to visit my parents this weekend.
She is going to study medicine.

lessons.heading: Future Continuous
lessons.text: Use for actions that will be in progress at a specific future time. Form: subject + will + be + verb-ing.
examples: I will be flying to New York at 8 PM tomorrow.
Don't call at 7 — I will be having dinner.
She'll be waiting for us at the station.
Will you be joining us for dinner?

lessons.heading: Future Perfect & Future Perfect Continuous
lessons.text: Use future perfect for actions completed by a future time (will have + past participle). Use future perfect continuous to emphasise duration up to a future time (will have been + verb-ing).
examples: I will have finished the report by 5 PM.
By next year she will have lived here for ten years.
I will have been working here for ten years next March.
She will have been studying for four hours by dinner.

exercises.sentence: I was ___ (watch) TV when you called.
She had already ___ (eat) when I arrived.
They had been ___ (wait) for an hour.
This time next week, I will be ___ (lie) on a beach.
By next year, I will have been ___ (work) here for five years.

title: Articles: A, An, The
description: When to use a, an, and the in English sentences.

lessons.heading: A vs An
lessons.text: Use 'a' before words that start with a consonant sound. Use 'an' before words that start with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u). Remember: it's about sound, not spelling!
examples: a cat
a university (sounds like 'yoo')
an apple
an hour (silent h)
an umbrella

lessons.heading: The — the Definite Article
lessons.text: Use 'the' when talking about something specific — something both you and the listener know about.
examples: The sun is bright. (there's only one sun)
Please close the door. (the listener knows which door)
I saw the movie you recommended.

lessons.heading: No Article
lessons.text: Don't use an article when talking about things in general, especially with plural or uncountable nouns.
examples: I like cats. (cats in general)
Water is important. (water in general)
She eats rice every day.

exercises.sentence: I saw ___ elephant at the zoo.
exercises.hint: elephant starts with a vowel sound
doctor starts with a consonant sound
h is silent, so it starts with a vowel sound
new starts with a consonant sound

title: Prepositions: In, On, At
description: Master the most common English prepositions of time and place.

lessons.heading: Prepositions of Place — In
lessons.text: Use 'in' for enclosed spaces, areas, cities, countries, and inside something.
examples: in the room
in New York
in India
in the box
in the ocean

lessons.heading: Prepositions of Place — On
lessons.text: Use 'on' for surfaces, streets, and electronic devices.
examples: on the table
on the wall
on Main Street
on TV
on the phone

lessons.heading: Prepositions of Place — At
lessons.text: Use 'at' for specific points, addresses, and events.
examples: at the bus stop
at 123 Main Street
at the cinema
at the door
at work

lessons.heading: Prepositions of Time — In, On, At
lessons.text: Use 'in' for months/years/seasons, 'on' for days/dates, 'at' for specific times.
examples: in January
in summer
on Monday
on January 15th
at 5 PM
at midnight
at night

title: Modal Verbs: Can, Must, Should
description: Use modal verbs to express ability, obligation, and advice.

lessons.heading: Can — Ability & Permission
lessons.text: Use 'can' to talk about ability (what you know how to do) and to ask for or give permission.
examples: I can swim. (ability)
She can speak three languages.
Can I open the window? (permission)
You can sit here. (permission)

lessons.heading: Must — Obligation & Necessity
lessons.text: Use 'must' to talk about rules, strong obligations, and things that are necessary. 'Must not' (mustn't) means it is forbidden.
examples: You must wear a seatbelt. (rule)
I must finish this today. (necessity)
You must not smoke here. (forbidden)

lessons.heading: Should — Advice & Recommendation
lessons.text: Use 'should' to give advice, opinions, and recommendations. 'Shouldn't' means it's not a good idea.
examples: You should see a doctor. (advice)
We should leave now. (recommendation)
You shouldn't eat too much sugar.

lessons.heading: Grammar Note
lessons.text: Modal verbs are followed by the base verb (no -s, no -ing, no 'to'). They don't change for he/she/it.
examples: He can swim. (not 'he cans')
She must go. (not 'she musts')
They should study more.

exercises.sentence: I ___ (ability not) come to the party.
You ___ (advice not) stay up too late.

title: Conjunctions
description: Connect words, phrases, and clauses with conjunctions like and, but, or, because, although.

lessons.heading: Coordinating Conjunctions: FANBOYS
lessons.text: Coordinating conjunctions connect equal parts — words with words, phrases with phrases, clauses with clauses. Remember FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So.
examples: I like tea and coffee.
She is tired but happy.
Do you want pizza or pasta?
He studied hard, so he passed the exam.

lessons.heading: Subordinating Conjunctions
lessons.text: Subordinating conjunctions connect a dependent clause to an independent clause. Common ones: because, although, while, when, if, since, unless, until.
examples: I stayed home because it was raining.
She went out although she was tired.
Call me when you arrive.
He waited until she finished.

lessons.heading: Correlative Conjunctions
lessons.text: Correlative conjunctions come in pairs: either…or, neither…nor, both…and, not only…but also, whether…or.
examples: Either you come now or we leave without you.
Neither John nor Mary was there.
She is both intelligent and hardworking.
Not only did he finish first, but he also broke the record.

exercises.sentence: I stayed home ___ it was raining.
___ you come now or we leave.
He studied hard, ___ he passed the exam.

title: Active & Passive Voice
description: Learn when and how to use the active and passive voice in English.

lessons.heading: Active vs Passive Voice
lessons.text: In active voice, the subject performs the action (subject → verb → object). In passive voice, the subject receives the action (object → be + past participle → by subject). Use active for direct, clear sentences. Use passive when the action or object is more important than who did it.
examples: Active: The cat ate the fish.
Passive: The fish was eaten by the cat.
Active: Shakespeare wrote Hamlet.
Passive: Hamlet was written by Shakespeare.

lessons.heading: Forming the Passive: be + past participle
lessons.text: The passive uses the correct form of 'be' + the past participle of the main verb. The tense of 'be' tells you when the action happened. You can include 'by + agent' or omit it if the agent is unknown or unimportant.
examples: The car is washed every week. (present simple passive)
The car was washed yesterday. (past simple passive)
The car will be washed tomorrow. (future simple passive)
The car has been washed. (present perfect passive)

lessons.heading: When to Use Passive Voice
lessons.text: Use passive when: (1) the agent is unknown, (2) the agent is obvious, (3) you want to emphasise the receiver of the action, (4) writing formal or scientific texts.
examples: My phone was stolen. (unknown agent)
He was arrested. (obvious — by police)
The experiment was conducted in 2020. (scientific writing)
The window was broken. (emphasising the window, not who broke it)

exercises.sentence: The fish ___ eaten by the cat. (passive)

title: Direct & Indirect Speech
description: Report what someone said using direct quotes and indirect (reported) speech.

lessons.heading: Direct Speech vs Indirect Speech
lessons.text: Direct speech uses the exact words someone said, placed in quotation marks. Indirect (reported) speech reports what someone said without using their exact words, and usually involves a tense shift.
examples: Direct: She said, 'I am tired.'
Indirect: She said that she was tired.
Direct: He asked, 'Do you like coffee?'
Indirect: He asked if I liked coffee.

lessons.heading: Tense Shifts in Reported Speech
lessons.text: When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, asked), the verb in the reported clause shifts back one tense: present → past, past → past perfect, will → would, can → could.
examples: 'I am happy.' → She said she was happy.
'I have finished.' → He said he had finished.
'I will call you.' → She said she would call me.
'I can swim.' → He said he could swim.

lessons.heading: Questions in Reported Speech
lessons.text: Reported questions use statement word order (not question order). Yes/no questions use 'if' or 'whether'. Wh-questions keep the question word. Do not use question marks.
examples: 'Do you like pizza?' → He asked if I liked pizza.
'Where do you live?' → She asked where I lived.
'Have you seen this movie?' → He asked whether I had seen that movie.

lessons.heading: Commands & Requests
lessons.text: Reported commands use 'told/asked + object + to + verb'. Negative commands use 'told/asked + object + not to + verb'.
examples: 'Sit down.' → He told me to sit down.
'Please help me.' → She asked me to help her.
'Don't be late.' → He told me not to be late.

exercises.sentence: Direct: 'I am happy.' → She said she ___ happy.
Direct: 'I have finished.' → He said he ___ finished.
exercises.hint: present perfect shifts to past perfect

exercises.sentence: Direct: 'I will call you.' → She said she ___ call me.
Direct: 'Do you like pizza?' → He asked ___ I liked pizza.
Direct: 'Sit down.' → He told me ___ sit down.

title: Conditionals (If Clauses)
description: Express real and unreal situations using conditionals — zero, first, second, third.

lessons.heading: Zero Conditional: General Truths
lessons.text: Use zero conditional for things that are always true — scientific facts and general rules. Form: if + present simple, present simple.
examples: If you heat ice, it melts.
If it rains, the grass gets wet.
If I am tired, I drink coffee.

lessons.heading: First Conditional: Real Future Possibilities
lessons.text: Use first conditional for real and possible situations in the future. Form: if + present simple, will + base verb.
examples: If it rains, I will take an umbrella.
If she studies hard, she will pass the exam.
If you don't hurry, you will miss the bus.

lessons.heading: Second Conditional: Unreal Present/Future
lessons.text: Use second conditional for imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future. Form: if + past simple, would + base verb.
examples: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.
If she were taller, she could be a model. (were for all subjects)
If I had more time, I would learn piano.

lessons.heading: Third Conditional: Unreal Past
lessons.text: Use third conditional for imaginary situations in the past — things that didn't happen. Form: if + had + past participle, would have + past participle.
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam. (but I didn't study)
If she had left earlier, she wouldn't have missed the train.
If we had known, we would have come earlier.

exercises.sentence: If it rains, I ___ take an umbrella.
If I won the lottery, I ___ travel the world.
If I had studied, I ___ have passed.
If she had left earlier, she wouldn't have ___ (miss) the train.

title: Question Tags
description: Turn statements into questions using short tags at the end: You like tea, don't you?

lessons.heading: The Basic Rule
lessons.text: A question tag is a short question at the end of a statement. If the statement is positive, the tag is negative. If the statement is negative, the tag is positive. The tag uses the same auxiliary verb (or do/does/did) as the main verb.
examples: You like coffee, don't you? (positive + negative tag)
She isn't coming, is she? (negative + positive tag)
He can swim, can't he?
They have finished, haven't they?

lessons.heading: Tense Matching
lessons.text: The tag must match the tense of the main verb. If there is no auxiliary verb, use do/does/did.
examples: You live here, don't you? (present, no auxiliary)
She lived there, didn't she? (past, no auxiliary)
He is coming, isn't he? (present continuous)
They have arrived, haven't they? (present perfect)

lessons.heading: Special Cases
lessons.text: With 'I am', use 'aren't I?' (not 'amn't I'). With 'Let's', use 'shall we?'. With imperatives, use 'will you?' or 'won't you?'.
examples: I am on time, aren't I?
Let's go for a walk, shall we?
Open the door, will you?
Don't be late, will you?

title: Sentence Structure (Complex)
description: Build complex sentences using independent and dependent clauses, relative clauses, and connectors.

lessons.heading: Simple, Compound & Complex Sentences
lessons.text: A simple sentence has one independent clause. A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a conjunction. A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
examples: Simple: I like coffee.
Compound: I like coffee, but my sister prefers tea.
Complex: I like coffee because it wakes me up.
Complex: The book that you recommended was excellent.

lessons.heading: Independent vs Dependent Clauses
lessons.text: An independent clause can stand alone (it's a complete sentence). A dependent clause cannot stand alone — it needs the independent clause to complete its meaning.
examples: Independent: I went to bed. (complete)
Dependent: because I was tired (not complete)
Complex: I went to bed because I was tired.
Dependent: although it was expensive (not complete)
Complex: She bought the dress although it was expensive.

lessons.heading: Relative Clauses
lessons.text: Relative clauses give extra information about a noun. Use who/that for people, which/that for things, where for places, when for times. Defining clauses are essential to meaning; non-defining clauses add extra info (with commas).
examples: The woman who lives next door is a doctor. (defining)
The book that I read was amazing. (defining)
My sister, who lives in London, is a teacher. (non-defining)
This is the house where I grew up.

exercises.sentence: I like coffee ___ it wakes me up.
The woman ___ lives next door is a doctor.
This is the house ___ I grew up.
The book ___ I read was amazing.
I went to bed ___ I was tired.

title: Degrees of Comparison
description: Compare things using positive, comparative, and superlative degrees of adjectives.

lessons.heading: The Three Degrees
lessons.text: Adjectives have three degrees: positive (the base form), comparative (comparing two things), and superlative (comparing one thing to all others).
examples: Positive: big, She is tall.
Comparative: bigger, She is taller than me.
Superlative: the biggest, She is the tallest in the class.

lessons.heading: Comparative: Comparing Two Things
lessons.text: For short adjectives (1-2 syllables), add -er + than. For long adjectives (3+ syllables), use more + adjective + than.
examples: small → smaller than
big → bigger than (double g)
happy → happier than (y→i)
beautiful → more beautiful than
expensive → more expensive than

lessons.heading: Superlative: One of Many
lessons.text: For short adjectives, add the + -est. For long adjectives, use the most + adjective.
examples: small → the smallest
big → the biggest
happy → the happiest
beautiful → the most beautiful
expensive → the most expensive

lessons.heading: Irregular Forms
lessons.text: Some common adjectives have completely irregular forms.
examples: good → better → the best
bad → worse → the worst
far → farther/further → the farthest/furthest
much/many → more → the most
little → less → the least

exercises.sentence: This is the ___ (good) restaurant in town.
He is the ___ (smart) student in the class.
This exam is ___ (bad) than the last one.
